en: I pay homage to that Unmanifest Lord, the single seed of the entire manifest world, whom the Sāṃkhyas proclaim as the sixfold source of wealth and debt, presided over by the Supreme Person and reckoned as the Sovereign.

Previously, the manifest (vyakta) was explained as having the unmanifest (avyakta) as its seed; for the most part, our questions cannot be understood by those of dull intellect without the application of the unmanifest. Therefore, since it is extremely difficult [for them] to understand, I shall explain the operation of the seeds (bīja-kriyā).
In calculation (yoga), there is addition when two quantities are both positive or both negative; otherwise, the difference between a positive and a negative quantity is indeed yoga.
Tell me quickly whether there are three or four figures, and whether they represent a loss or a gain combined;
you understand the addition of gains and losses both when they are separate and when they are combined.
[Upajāti; ab;

cd=7] BG 5: Here, the initial syllables of the unmanifested forms (*avyakta*) should be written for the sake of illustration. Likewise, those that have undergone reduction (*ūnagata*) should be provided with an upper dot (*ūrdhvabindu*). [Prose]
BG 6: Even when [the planets] are thus separated;
BG 7: That which is being subtracted becomes a debt (ṛṇatva), while its own nature is loss (kṣaya); their conjunction is as previously stated.
From three, subtract two; from one's own, subtract one's own; and from debt, subtract debt. Having performed these subtractions individually and collectively, tell me quickly the remainder.
In the case of one's own or another's property, there is the loss of that property upon the destruction of the debt; in the case of destroying one's own debt, there is a reduction [of the interest].
Wealth is destroyed by wealth, debt by debt; the two are neutralized by the third. What would one's own wealth be to a debtor?
And this is also explained in the case of division by parts.
Eight forms divided by four forms, wealth by wealth, debt by debt,
and debt by wealth— what would one's own wealth become when divided by debt? Tell me this quickly, if you wish to understand.
In the case of one's own property and debt, the property belongs to its own root; however, in the case of wealth and debt, there is no root for decay, because that [decay] is not an act of creation.
O friend, tell me quickly the square of the three forms of wealth and of loss (BG 14);
and tell me quickly, separately, the square roots of the nine numbers consisting of both positive and negative values (BG 15). [Upajāti]
In the yoga of zero, there are six kinds of zero;
likewise, when subtracted from zero, a positive or negative quantity undergoes its opposite.
The three qualities of one's own nature lead to destruction and are void; tell me, what could be joined with the void, and what would remain when the void is subtracted?

In the case of killing and so forth, the void (0) of space (kha) is divided by the void (0) of space (kha); when there is a killing by the void (0), the result is a void (0), and the heap is also divided by the void (0).
Tell me, O friend, the square root of two multiplied by itself, divided by three, then divided by zero, and then the cube of zero. (BG 19)

Just as in the infinite and imperishable multitude of beings, there may be dissolution and creation during many cycles of time— even when this group has entered the void-like sky or has emerged from it— so too is it with this transformation.
Color is of six kinds:
*yāvattāvat*, *kālakas*, *nīlakas*, and other colors such as yellow (*pīta*) and red (*lohita*).
These and others are designated by the names of the unmanifested (*avyakta*) for the purpose of enumeration, having been conceptualized by the best of teachers. (Śālinī meter)
Among them, yoga is the internal state, as well as the distinct abiding of those of the same class and those of different classes.
O friend, there is one positive unknown (sva-avyakta) of uniform form, a pair of negative unknowns (dhana-avyakta-yugma), and eight negative forms (vi-rūpa-aṣṭaka).
When these two sides are combined, tell me quickly: what would the result be after reversing the positive and negative values and then summing them?
What would be the result if the three groups of wealth and the unmanifest, together with their three forms, were joined with the pair of destruction and the unmanifest?
[In the *Bhujaṅgaprayāta* meter;
cd = 25] O Bhagavatī, having subtracted six negative unknowns along with one positive unit from eight positive unknowns and two negative unknowns, tell me quickly what remains.
But when there is a conflict between form (rūpa) and color (varṇa), the color of those [syllables] of two, three, or more [consonants] belonging to the same class shall prevail.

In the case of multiplication, however, the cube of that group and so forth shall be the result; and when there is the multiplication of unlike classes, the quotient and the remainder shall be treated exactly like integers. Whatever has been stated regarding explicit calculation in arithmetic applies here as well.

The multiplicand should be set down separately, equal in number to the parts of the multiplier; then, by those parts multiplied in sequence and combined according to the stated rule, the method for multiplying the parts as explained for manifest square roots should likewise be considered here for the multiplication of irrational square roots.

O learned one, having first multiplied the five-fold set of *yāvat-tāvat* by the three-fold set of *yāvat-tāvat* increased by two, and then by the single form of *vi-eka-rūpa*, quickly state the product or the multiplier, having alternatively treated the positive and negative values as their own respective debts.
When subtracted from the dividend, the remainder is purified; having fallen from its own places, it is restored to its positions in due order.
Whatever multipliers and whatever forms correspond to the quotients obtained in the division, those shall be the values here.
[Śālinī] O friend, tell me the square of four unknowns (avyakta) diminished by six units. [Śālinī-ab]
Having taken the terms from those [groups] that are divisible, one should apply the double product of the two-fold multiplication to each pair;
then, having taken the term "rūpa" from the remainder, one should discard it if there are further rūpas, and the remainder remains exactly as it is.
[Upajāti] The colors are yāvattāvat, kālaka, and nīlaka, and the wealth is three, five, and seven.

How many [results] would there be if those [quantities], measured by two, three, and one, were combined with or subtracted from the [coefficients] located in the destruction-place? [The answer is: The triad of *yāvat*, *tāvat*, and the constant is negative; the two time-terms (*kālakau*) and the blue term (*nīlaka*) are positive. These are increased by their own forms and multiplied by those same [coefficients] doubled in measure. What would be the product resulting from their multiplication? What would be the quotient when that product is divided by the multiplicand? Furthermore, tell me the square of the multiplicand and the square root of that square.
[In the *mandākrāntā* meter,
consisting of six *karaṇīs*:
Having constructed the great *karaṇī* for the square of the sum and the small one as twice the square root;
In another method of calculation, one should multiply the square of these two by their sum and then divide [the result] by that same sum, as if dealing with square roots.

When the smaller number has been divided by the larger, the resulting quotient is increased by one and decreased by one; these two values, multiplied by their own respective roots, are the products for the smaller number.
In another method, these two values may exist sequentially, or they may stand separately if no square root exists.
O friend, tell me the sum and the difference of the two karaṇīs numbered two and eight, and those numbered three and five;
and after reflecting for a long time, O friend, if you know the sixfold [results] of the karaṇīs numbered three and seven.
The multiplicand consists of two square roots having the numbers two, three, and eight as their respective qualities, and [the multiplier] is the number three together with five units.
Quickly state the product when the multiplier is twenty-five, or when the two square roots are thirty-three.
Furthermore, if the square of a negative unit is being computed for the sake of establishing it as a square root, there shall be a subtraction.
Likewise,
for a negative quantity (ṛṇātmanīkā), the root of the karaṇī is the decrease for the purpose of determining the square;
having repeatedly performed the reversal of the status of debt and wealth in the karaṇī desired for the extraction of the square root.
One should multiply such a divisor by the dividend and divide; this single operation continues until the divisor becomes a surd (*karaṇī*).
Then, the surds contained within the dividend are divided by that [divisor]; if the resulting surds are produced by addition, [they remain as they are].
The square roots of the desired quantities should be found separately by means of the rule for subtraction, in whatever manner is required.
A *yoga-karaṇī* divided by a group [of numbers] shall be purified; the desired square roots of its square are obtained.
Having performed their respective squares, these *karaṇīs* indeed become multiplied by the previously obtained [root], and thus these *karaṇīs* remain distinct.

O learned one, tell me quickly and individually: what is the product of those Karaṇīs measured by two, three, and five; and likewise the products of the numbers two and three; and of those measured by six, five, two, and three? (Vasantatilakā and Upajāti)
O friend, the verses of these works—numbering eighteen, eight, and two—are composed with great skill.
If there are square roots in a group, or two equal square roots, or many square roots,
one should subtract the square root of the sum of the squares from the remaining squares, both added and subtracted.

If there are two square roots (karaṇīs) in that half, then those which are multiple roots among them should be treated as square units (rūpas). If there are further remaining roots in the square, this process should be repeated.
If a negative root (ṛṇa-karaṇī) occurs in the calculation, one should treat it as a positive root (dhana-karaṇī) and proceed with the solution.
The square roots of these two, which are negative in nature, are desired at the base; they must be understood by one of keen intellect.
Tell me the square root of the difference between the squares of three and seven.
The *karaṇīs* measured by two, three, and five, whether they fall under their own respective debts or under reversed wealth and debt—
tell me their square, and the square root thereof, O friend, if you know the sixfold method of *karaṇīs*.
The segments of *karaṇīs* measured by the sum of one and so forth shall constitute the square quantity.
In a group consisting of three surds (*karaṇī*), there are terms identical in form to two of those surds;
in a group of six surds, there are such terms for three, four, and five [surds] respectively, in ten and fifteen [units].
If one disregards the square of the integer term (*rūpa*) and seeks the root otherwise, it is nowhere valid.
When the square root is about to be produced,
those subtrahends (apavarta) which would result from dividing the small fourfold multiplier by a unit should be subtracted;
and those square roots obtained through the division are also [the subtrahends].
If those [roots] do not exist according to the remaining rule, then that [result] is false.
O learned one, tell me: what would be the square root of that number in which the *karaṇī* terms are measured by thirty-two, twenty-four, and eight, and are increased by ten units?
In a group where the surds (karaṇī) are equal to four times fifteen, eighteen, and twenty-three,
increased by ten forms— tell me, what would be the square root of that?
[Āryā] Where there are eight, fifty-six, sixty, and three surds in the square.
"Endowed with ten forms, tell me what its root might be.
"Where four times the qualities, the sun, the lunar days, Rudras, Nāgas, and seasons are to be applied in the Kṛta period—
along with the Viśavas and the forms— tell me that position, if you have confidence in your skill regarding the seed-syllable."
If the *karaṇīs* are equal to forty, eighty, and two hundred, and are endowed with seventeen forms, tell me: what is their value in the calculation? [Upagīti] [The Explanation of the Kuṭṭaka]

The dividend, the divisor, and the additive may be reduced by some common factor at the outset, provided such a possibility exists for the purpose of the *kuṭṭaka* (pulverizer). However, that by which the dividend and divisor are divided must not divide the additive; otherwise, this problem is indeed defective. [Śālinī meter] When two numbers are divided by each other, whatever remains shall be their common divisor (*apavartana*).
Those two, the dividend and the divisor, when divided by that common factor, are designated as "firm" (dṛḍha).
One should divide those two firm dividend and divisor by each other until the dividend here becomes a single unit (rūpa).
The resulting quotients should be placed one below the other, and the subtrahend (kṣepa) should likewise be placed at the end; zero should be used with the penultimate [quotient].

When the upper [value] is multiplied by its own [multiplier], added to the last [value], and the last is discarded, it will repeatedly result in a pair of quantities. The upper [value], divided by the firm divisor, shall be the quotient; the other shall be the multiplier by the subtractor (haraka).
Thus it is here at that very time when those [quotients] are equal; if the quotients are unequal, then [the process continues].
The two values obtained by the method of *āgata* (addition) are to be purified by their own respective divisors; thus, they remain as the remainders measured by those divisors.
In the rule for *kuṭṭaka* (pulverizer), the multiplier (*guṇa*) remains the same even when the additive (*yuti*) and the divisor (*bhājya*) are reduced by a common factor (*apavarta*).
Furthermore, that multiplier shall be multiplied by the factor used for the reduction of the additive and the divisor.
When the result born of addition (yoga) is pure from the outset, the attainment of the qualities (guṇa) occurs immediately; when it is born of subtraction (viyoga), they occur later.
Likewise, when the result is born of multiplication by a positive number (dhana-bhājya), it is so; and when born of multiplication by a negative number (ṛṇa-bhājya), it shall be the same.
The wise person should take the quotient and multiplier as equal when performing subtraction;
however, when the dividend is diminished by the divisor, the quotient and multiplier remain as before.
When subtracting, the quotient is increased by the remainder of the subtraction of the divisor, but in the case of addition, it is decreased.

Alternatively, when the additive and the dividend have been reduced by their common divisor, the multiplier is as before; then the quotient is obtained from the dividend after it has been multiplied by the multiplier, increased by the remainder, and divided.
Or, where there is no additive, or where the additive, divided by the divisor, results in an integer, [the same process applies].
The quotient is to be known as the void (śūnya) [of the divisor]; the remainder there, divided by the *hara*, is the result.
When joined with their respective desired and undesired hara, those two may result in the attainment of qualities in many ways.
O mathematician, tell me quickly that multiplier which, when added to twenty-one, becomes two hundred and sixty-five; and when divided by two hundred minus five, yields a quotient of exact purity.
One hundred minus ninety, or one hundred plus ninety, divided by sixty-three—tell me that remainder clearly if you are truly skilled in *kuṭṭaka* (pulverizer).
[Rathoddhatā] If it is subtracted from one hundred, the remainder is nine; if added to one hundred, the remainder is nineteen. Dividing these two results by sixty-three, what would the residue be?
Tell me that quotient clearly if you are proficient in *kuṭṭaka*. [Upajāti]
O mathematician, tell me separately that multiplier by which sixty is either increased or decreased such that it becomes exactly divisible by thirteen, leaving no remainder.
By whom were the eighteen qualities increased by ten, or decreased by ten?
They provide a pure portion extracted by eleven, which,
when multiplied by five and increased by twenty-three, results in the total.
Or if they were divided by three and then subtracted from them, what would be the remainder? What quality would that possess?

O calculator, quickly tell me that multiplier by which five multiplied, joined with zero, and increased by sixty-five, or alternatively, thirteen divided [by that same multiplier], results in a number without a remainder.
Having conceptualized the distinction between the two as being merely a projection and a purification, those who perceive their qualities, causes, and attainments as separate [are mistaken].
When the desired [quotient] is multiplied by the subtraction-correction and divided by its own divisor, those two results are obtained. Then,
the remainder of the deficient seconds (kalā) should be treated as the dividend, sixty as the divisor, and the omitted days (kudināni) as the divisor.
The result produced by that [multiplier] shall be the *kalās*; the *guṇas* shall be the *liptā-agra*. From this, the *kalā-lava-agra* [is derived].
In this same manner, above that, the days for the Sun and Moon are obtained from the *adhimāsa-agra* and *avama-agra* respectively.
If there is a single divisor but two different multipliers, then the sum of the multipliers should be taken as the dividend.
The "summit" (agra) is that which has been made the first [quotient] as previously described; it is known as the "conjoined" (saṃśliṣṭa) and is the clear pulverizer (kuṭṭaka).
What number, when multiplied by five and divided by sixty-three, leaves a remainder of seven?
Furthermore, that same number, when multiplied by ten and divided by sixty-three, yields fourteen as the summit (agra). Tell me this number.
If the square of the desired small root, when multiplied by its own nature (prakṛti), is increased or decreased by some number such that it yields a square root,
then that additive is called the "small root" (mūla) as either positive or negative; and they call that [original] root the "greater root" (jyeṣṭha-mūla).

Having set down the subtrahends for the least and the greatest [roots], and having placed those or other [subtrahends] beneath them in sequence, many roots are to be derived from these through successive operations; therefore, the method of derivation is now described.
The square of the greatest and the least [roots] is the "thunderbolt" (vajra); their sum is the "least" (hrasva); and the product of the two least [roots] is the "strike" (āhati) by nature.

The square root of the product [of the two numbers], when increased by the square root of the difference between their squares, shall be the sum; the square root of that [sum], when diminished by the square root of the difference between their squares, shall be the difference.
Or else, the difference between the square roots of the product and the constant term, or the product of the smaller [roots] multiplied by the original constant, [shall be the result].

The product of the two largest [roots], their difference, the largest [root], and here also the product of the augment (kṣepa)—the augment multiplied by the square of the chosen number (iṣṭa) shall be the augment when divided by that chosen number; these are the two roots. Alternatively, the augment multiplied by the multiplier is then the square root of the multiplier.
Or one may divide by the difference between the square of the chosen number (*iṣṭavarga*) and the original number (*prakṛti*).
Twice the square of the chosen number is the "lesser" (*kaniṣṭha*); that is the root, and when increased by one, it becomes the other.
Then, [the calculation for] the highest infinity here is likewise from the perspective of mental cultivation and from the perspective of what is desired. [In verse form:
O mathematician, tell me: which square, when multiplied by eight and increased by one, becomes a perfect square?
Or which square, multiplied by eleven and increased by one, becomes a perfect square, my friend?
Having made the short and long values the dividend-increment and the divisor respectively,
one should determine the multiplier (*guṇa*) such that, when subtracted from the original constant (*prakṛti*),
the remainder is small, or else the square of the multiplier minus the constant is small.
That [quotient], however, is diminished by the *kṣepa*; the *kṣepa* is subtracted from the *prakṛti*.
The quotient obtained is the short term; from that, the long term is derived repeatedly.
Having discarded the previous terms and the *kṣepas*, they call this the *cakravāla* method.
In this way, when increased by four, two, and one, they become two distinct square roots.
The process for finding the square roots of the [quantities] increased by four and two, as well as the value of the constant term increased by one, is as follows:
O friend, what is that square which, multiplied by sixty-seven and increased by one, and then multiplied by sixty-one and increased by one?
If that which is both the root and the manifestation were entirely present in your mind, O dear one, then speak; it would be like a spreading creeper.
In the case of the purification of a square number, if the sum of the factors is not a multiplier, it is designated as a "residue" (khila).

If there is no residue, the square number is divided in two ways by its square root. [Anuṣṭubh] If the sum of the factors is not a multiplier, it is designated as a "residue" (khila) in the purification of a square number. If there is no residue, the square number is divided in two ways by its square root.

The superior short word is twofold; then, for the purification of the form, the two words for the purification of the form are established as before. The square of thirteen is one less; what would be its square?
Or, tell me: what square, when multiplied by eight and increased by one, has ten as its square root?
What square, when multiplied by six and increased by three, or else increased by twelve, remains a perfect square?
Or, what square, when added to seventy-five, or to three hundred, becomes a perfect square?

When the square root is to be known by one's own intellect for the purpose of purifying many subtrahends, one should apply the method of *bhāvanā* (successive approximation) arising from the square, the subtrahend,
and the square root to achieve infinity.
When the square has been subtracted from the multiplicand, one should divide that [remainder] by the square root.
BG 83: Tell me, what is that square which, when multiplied by thirty-two and increased by one, has ten as its square root?
BG 84: When the desired divisor has been applied twice to the additive, and it is diminished or increased by the desired [divisor], and then halved;
the first [result] divided by the square root of the multiplier gives the smaller and larger roots respectively.
What number, when multiplied by nine and increased by fifty-two, is its own square?
Or what number, when quadrupled and increased by thirty-three, is its own square? What number, when multiplied by thirteen and decreased by thirteen, is its own square?
Or let it be stated as a square increased by thirteen.
(BG 86c) Which square, multiplied by five and diminished by twenty-one, would be a perfect square?
Tell me, if you know the method for negative principal numbers. (BG 87a–c)
This concise calculation concerning the application of seeds has indeed been stated.
Therefore, I shall now explain the seed-method, which brings joy to mathematicians. [The Reduction of Indeterminate Equations with One Unknown]

To whatever extent the measure of the indeterminate mass is to be conceived, that very amount should be assigned by one performing the operation. Both sides should be equalized with effort—by subtracting, adding, multiplying, or dividing.
Then, one should eliminate one indeterminate from the other side and the constants from the remaining side.
In the case of the remaining unmanifest [quantities], one should not extract the remainder of the form; rather, the manifest measure arises from the manifest heap.

(Śālinī) Even for two or more unmanifest [quantities] here, one should calculate the measure by multiplying or dividing by two or more, or by adding or subtracting according to one's own intellect, having thus understood the manifest in some instance. (Śālinī)
One possesses three hundred gold pieces and six horses; another possesses ten horses, each of equal value to the gold pieces.
Furthermore, one has a debt of one hundred gold pieces. Are these two men of equal wealth? What, then, is the value of a horse?
Or, if the second man’s wealth were equal to twice the square root of the first man’s wealth, would they be equal?
The first [horse] is worth three times its value in gold, or otherwise from another source; tell me the price of each horse individually.

O friend, the measurements for the ruby, the pure sapphire, and the pearl are five, eight, and seven respectively for one [type], and for the other, they are seven, nine, and six; such is the number of those gems.
O wise one, these two possess equal wealth, consisting of ninety and sixty *rūpakas* respectively; therefore, O expert in seeds, quickly state the prices for each of those gems.

[Śārdūlavikrīḍita] One says: "Give me ten; for by means of that wealth, O friend, I shall become twice as great as you. Another says: "If you give me ten, I shall be six times greater than you. Tell me, between those two, what is my share of the wealth?
[Siṃhoddhatā] Eight rubies, ten sapphires, and a hundred pearls— which were purchased at equal value for your earrings by me for your sake— O beloved,
tell me the individual price of each of those three gems separately, if you are indeed skilled in calculation here, O auspicious one! For the total sum of their combined values is seventy-five.
Five parts from the swarm of bees went to the *kadamba* tree, three parts to the *śilīndhra*; their separation was tripled at the *kuṭaja*, O deer-eyed one, while another remained hovering.
O beloved, tell me the number of bees as they wander here and there in the sky, summoned by messengers, drawn simultaneously by the fragrance of both the *ketaka* and the *mālatī*.
Having subtracted the square of the fruit from the wealth given for five hundred, the remainder is equal to the time given for one thousand; and the fruits of those two are likewise equal. [Āryā]
Having subtracted the square root of the fruit from the wealth given by one hundred and one,

the remainder is equal to the time and the fruit for those two who have each given five hundred. [Āryā] Eight rubies, ten sapphires, a hundred pearls, and five excellent diamonds are the wealth of four jewel-merchants.

Out of the power of attachment and affection, they each gave one of their own treasures from among their personal wealth to one another until they all possessed equal riches; tell me separately, my friend, the values of those jewels.
When a year has passed, including the interest and sub-interest, five hundred was given as principal;
the amount received was double that minus sixteen. Tell me, what was the principal? [Āryā]
If three hundred and ninety units of wealth were given in three portions— namely five, two, and four hundred—

over seventeen months and five days respectively, and the same amount was obtained with equal interest over those same periods, tell me the number of portions such that the result is the same for all three.
At the entry into the city, he gave ten times ten, doubled again, and upon departure he gave the remainder after consuming one-tenth;
thus he gave exactly ten in each of the three cities. Tell me, what was that initial amount which became tripled?

"O merchant, if for one *dramma* you have three and a half measures of rice, eight measures of mung beans, and thirteen *kākiṇīs*, then take these and give me two parts of rice along with one part of mung beans. Let us go quickly, O swift eater; for our caravan leader will depart ahead of us."
Which three numbers, when increased by one-half, one-fifth, and one-ninth respectively, become equal;
and which, when decreased by two other parts, have sixty as their remainder—tell me those.
Thirteen and five likewise are the measures of the two forearms;
the ground here is unknown—its extent is four [units]. Tell me quickly, O Bhūmi, what the fruit of this ground is.
The base is fifteen *karaṇīs* less one arm, and the other side is six *karaṇīs*;
the ground is eighteen *karaṇīs* less one *rūpa*. Tell me the perpendicular height.
Tell me those four piles that have equal differences between their terms,
such that either their sum or the sum of their cubes is equal to the sum of their squares.
If there should be a triangular field whose area is equal to its side,
or likewise equal to the product of its two sides and its hypotenuse;
If the square of two numbers when added together becomes a square, and their square when subtracted becomes a square,
and their product becomes a cube— quickly tell me those two quantities, if you are indeed skilled in calculation.
If you know those two numbers for which the cube equals the sum of their squares and the square equals the sum of their cubes,
then I consider you the best among those who know the secrets of numbers.
Friend, tell me: in a triangular field where the base is equal to the side, one arm is fifteen units and the other is thirteen; what is the length of the perpendicular there?

O calculator, if a bamboo pole measuring two or three cubits on level ground is broken in one place by the force of the wind, and its tip touches the earth at a distance measured in royal cubits, tell me: how many cubits from the base was it broken?
In a certain pond whose waters were agitated by wheels and cranes, the tip of a lotus bud was seen rising one span above the surface;
it moved very slowly when struck by the wind and sank back into that pair of hands. O calculator, tell me quickly the depth of the water.

Suppose a certain monkey goes from a tree one hundred cubits high to a pond at a distance of one hundred *yuga*s; then, having crossed over, he flies swiftly from the tree toward the opposite shore, rising slightly above the path of hearing (*śruti*).
If, O learned one, their speeds are thus equal as they fly, and you possess great skill in calculation, tell me quickly: how much distance has he traversed?

Tell me the length of the plumb-lines for two bamboos, fifteen and ten cubits in height respectively, whose intermediate points are unknown and which are joined by a cord running from the root of one to the tip of the other.

[The extraction of the middle term: When the remainder of the unmanifest (avyakta) class and so forth is multiplied by some desired quantity, it should be added to those two sides so that they may yield a square root;
furthermore, this is done by means of the square root of the unmanifest side.
In this way, by performing the same operation on the manifest side, the measure of the unmanifest is indeed obtained.
If it does not result in a perfect square among the cubes and squares, then this should be understood through one's own intellect.
If the square of the unknown (avyakta) side is negative, it should be made positive by treating the negative as positive;
and in some cases, that measure of the unknown is of two kinds.
One should multiply the two sides by forms equal to four times the square of the class;
then one should add to those very two [sides] forms equal to the square of the previous indeterminate [quantity].
The root of the lotus petals has been reached by a swarm of bees; eight parts of the entire group, plus one bee as the ninth part, have gone to the jasmine.
At night, greedy for fragrance, that single bee is trapped in the center of the lotus; tell me, my beloved, the total number of bees as they hum in resonance.

Enraged in battle, Pārtha aimed a multitude of arrows for the slaying of Karṇa; having warded off that mass of shafts with half [of his own], he struck down his horses with four arrow-heads, Śalya with six arrows, and then cut through his parasol, banner, and bow with three more, and his head with a single arrow—how many did Arjuna discharge in all?
The first term of a series is indeed the square root of the common difference; the sum of those [terms] is the result.
The product of the common difference and the number of terms, increased by one-seventh of itself, is the sum of the series. Tell me, what are the common difference and the number of terms?
By what number has the heap been divided, such that when increased by ten million or decreased [by it],
and then squared and added its own square root, the result is ninety times zero?
Let it be stated what number, when increased by its own half, multiplied by zero (0), squared, added to itself,
divided by its own square roots, and [finally] divided by itself, results in fifteen.
O learned one, what number is such that when multiplied by twelve and increased by its own cube,
it becomes equal to its square multiplied by six and increased by thirty-five?
If a certain number, when multiplied by two hundred, added to its own square, and divided by two,
results in a value that— when diminished by one— is equal to the square of the square of that original number (ten thousand, 10,000),
tell me that number if you know the operation of algebra (*bījagaṇita*).
In the midst of the forest, eight parts of a monkey, filled with passion, leap about;
and on the mountain, twelve of you who are thrilled by the echoing resonance of the "brūt" cry—how many are you? Tell me!
A troop of monkeys, diminished by one-third and then squared, has entered a thicket;
a monkey seen climbing a branch—tell me, how many are there?
The shadow of a twelve-finger gnomon is diminished by one-third of a karṇa.
O calculator, tell me quickly: it has become fourteen finger-breadths in length.
What are the four heaps? They are the root-slaves (mūla-dās) joined with two [others].
As for the eighteen [planets] associated with each pair, they are the "near-killing" (āsanna-ghāta) ones.
From the sum of all the roots increased by eleven, one obtains the square root (pada).
"O friend, knower of seeds, thirteen have been born; tell them to me."
The multiplier by which the addition for the product [is obtained] from the addition for the sum is the square root of the subsequent [term];
the unknown quantities (avyakta-rāśayaḥ) should be assumed as squares diminished by the addition.
When the field is equal to the lunar days and the nails (twenty-five), what fault could there be in that? What is the scriptural authority for it?
And let the logical justification for this established calculation be told.
When the product of two unknowns is doubled and combined with the sum of the squares of the differences of their positive and negative extremes,
it becomes equal to the sum of the squares of those two unknowns.

O friend, tell me: in any field whatsoever, given the hypotenuse, the sine, and the ear (the other side), where the hypotenuse is three units less than the base and the sine is one unit less, what is the difference between the hypotenuse and the ear?
The difference between the square of the sum of two quantities and the sum of their squares shall be equal to twice their product,
just as in the case of two unknowns; likewise,
the difference between four times the product and the square of the sum [is equal to twice the difference of the quantities].
Just as when two unknown quantities are equal after being added to different constants.
Tell me of those whose fame reaches forty million ears,
and in whom there are one hundred and twenty crores of arms.
Tell me separately about those for whom there are fifty-six crores of yogas as their lifespan,
as well as six hundred multiplied by seven, namely forty-two thousand.
[Equalizing multiple unknowns:
One should subtract the first unknown from the other side and the remaining forms from the first side;
when there are many measures for a single unknown, the measure of that one unknown will be found in the other side divided by the first [unknown].
When the subtraction of the equalized [coefficients] has been performed, the measures of the other two unknowns (varṇas) besides those two must be established.
In the final measure, the multiplier and quotient obtained by the method of pulverizer (kuṭṭaka) are the measures for the divisor and the dividend varṇas respectively.
If there are other [unknown] quantities remaining to be divided, one should assume an arbitrary value for their measure and solve;

then, by means of inverse elevation (*vilomaka-uttāpana*), the measures of the other unknowns are found. If the measure is thus different, the pulverizer (*kuṭṭaka*) must be performed again here; having raised the last unknown by that [value], one should raise it in reverse from the first.
O friend, the values of one [ruby], another [sapphire], and pearl are five, eight, and seven respectively; those of the other two [emerald and diamond] are seven, nine, and six.
Thus, the total number of these gems is ninety-two. O wise one, tell me quickly the prices for each type of gem so that these two may possess equal wealth according to their knowledge of seeds.

[Śārdūlavikrīḍita] One says: "Give me a hundred; for by wealth, O friend, I shall become twice as great as you. Another says: "If you give me ten, I shall be six times greater than you. Tell me, between those two, what will be my share of the wealth?
There are four horses whose value is measured by five, five, five, and five auspicious limbs; and there are camels whose wealth is measured by two, seven, four, and one.
Their mules and bulls are numbered respectively by seven, one, two, and one eye of the moon. Tell me immediately the prices of these horses and the rest, for all of them possess equal wealth.
Three *pārāvata* birds [are killed] by three; five *sārasa* cranes by five;
seven [other birds] by seven; nine swans by nine; and three peacocks by three.
"A dram is obtained for a dram; bring a hundred [drams] for a hundred, O Lord of the Earth, for the sake of diversion with these pigeons and other birds."
What number, when divided by six, leaves a remainder of five; when divided by five, leaves a remainder of four;
when divided by four, leaves a remainder of three; and when divided by three, leaves a remainder of two?
When [the number of] some [objects] has been multiplied by five, seven, or nine and divided by twenty,
the remainders are the forms increased by one, and the quotients are the sums of the remainders.

What would one with a single numerator divided by two be? What would one with a numerator of two divided by three be? And what would one with a numerator of three divided by five be? Indeed, the results obtained are exactly like that.

O learned one, you who are a lion amidst the herd of elephants that are the masters of the *kuṭṭaka* (pulverizer) method: tell me, which two numbers, when divided by five and six respectively, have remainders of one and two; whose difference, when divided by two and three, has a remainder of nine; whose sum, when divided by nine, has a remainder of five; and whose product, when divided by seven, has a remainder of six? (If you know, then speak.)
What number, when multiplied by nine and seven and then divided by thirty, has a sum of remainders that,
when added to the sum of the quotients, equals twenty-six?
What is the heap multiplied by three, seven, and nine, divided by thirty, such that even the sum of its remainders, when divided by thirty, yields eleven as the remainder?
O expert in pulverizer (kuṭṭaka), tell me quickly that number which, when multiplied by twenty-three and divided separately by sixty and eighty, results in a sum of one hundred.

In this case, the desired measure of the greater number situated in the dividend (bhājya) should not be assumed as the quotient obtained; for if it were so done, the calculation would deviate from the truth.
What is the heap multiplied by five and divided by thirteen;
when the quotient is added to the original heap, it results in thirty? Tell me that quickly.
Suppose there are those who, having bought six hundred and eighty fruits for fifty coins each,
sell them again and keep the remainder, paying five coins for each one;
since they have become equal in their coins, what is their buying and what is their selling?
[The extraction of the middle term contained within the equalization of multiple colors:
If the first square (the leading term) remains after the subtraction of like terms has been performed on one side, its square root is taken as described above;
the square root of the other side is found by means of the "prakṛti" (leading coefficient), and then the procedure for the equalization of those two is repeated.
If the object were not [present] according to its own class-nature, then it would be equal to that which was produced by another color.
Having formed the other side [of the equation] and another measure through the square of the *prakṛti*,
and likewise the initial value through the square of the *prakṛti* so that the object may be obtained, the wise should reflect upon this in many ways.
For the sake of awakening those of dull intellect, the gods, beginning with their own progenitor, have indeed expanded this seed of intelligence, which possesses various colors and companions.
